title: Away Fixture
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Maya had worn her boots to bed the night before the trial, just to break them in, and her mum had laughed so hard she'd had to sit down on the stairs. Now, standing on the touchline of the county ground with rain needling sideways into her face, Maya wished she'd worn two extra pairs of socks instead.

There were thirty-one girls trying out for eleven places. Maya counted them twice while the coach, a wiry woman called Ferris who blew her whistle like she was cross with it, read names off a clipboard gone soft with damp. Maya's name was somewhere in the middle. Priya Shah's was near the top, which felt about right, because Priya had been the best player at their old primary school and was, infuriatingly, also kind about it.

"You'll be fine," Priya said, bouncing on her toes beside her. "You're quick."

"You're better," Maya said, and meant it, though she hated saying it out loud.

The first twenty minutes were a blur of slipping studs and a ball that seemed to weigh twice as much once the rain soaked into it. Maya mistimed a tackle in the fourth minute and ended up sitting in a puddle with her socks flooded and her pride worse off than that. Ferris didn't shout. She just made a small mark on her clipboard, and Maya spent the next ten minutes convinced that mark had her name written under it in permanent ink.

But something happens to you when you've already fallen down once. The fear of it goes, because it's already happened, and there's nothing left to protect. Maya stopped thinking about the mark on the clipboard and started thinking about the ball. She began reading the game the way her dad had taught her in the park on Sunday mornings — not watching the ball but watching the space it was about to arrive in. She won it back twice near the halfway line. She set Priya up for a goal with a pass that surprised her more than it surprised Priya, who spun round with her arms out, grinning through the rain like it wasn't fifty percent trying to drown them.

With four minutes left, the ball came to Maya on the edge of the box, and for one long second the whole pitch seemed to go quiet, the way it does in the stories, and she thought: this is the moment. She shot. It cannoned off the underside of the crossbar, spun on the wet grass, and rolled agonisingly wide.

Ferris blew the final whistle without any particular expression on her face at all.

The trialists trudged off in twos and threes, peeling off wet bibs, breath steaming in the cold. Maya found herself walking next to Priya, both of them soaked through, both of them saying nothing for a while, which was unusual for either of them.

"You'll get picked," Priya said eventually. "That pass was better than anything I did."

"You scored," Maya said. "I hit the bar."

"Hitting the bar isn't missing," Priya said. "It's the same as scoring, only the metal got there first."

Maya turned that over as they reached the gate where the parents were waiting under a scatter of umbrellas, engines already running, radiators steaming faintly in the wet air. She thought about the mark on Ferris's clipboard, and the shot that hadn't gone in, and Priya's strange, generous arithmetic about the crossbar. The list wouldn't go up until Monday. There was nothing to do now but wait, and carry her boots home still full of rain, and not know, for two more days, which version of herself Ferris had written down.
prompts: What happens to Maya in the fourth minute of the trial, and how does Ferris react?
Why does Maya's mood change after she falls in the puddle? Use evidence from the text.
Do you think Priya's comment about the crossbar is fair? What would you have said to Maya at the gate?

vocabulary.meaning: people trying out for a team or place, to see if they are good enough
in a way that makes you annoyed or frustrated
hit something hard and bounced off it forcefully
kind and willing to give credit or be fair to someone

title: Eight Arms and No Bones
author: Oakman Academy
body:
If you want to understand how strange an octopus really is, start with its blood. Yours is red because it carries oxygen in a protein built around iron. An octopus's blood is blue, because its oxygen-carrying protein, called haemocyanin, is built around copper instead. This isn't just a cosmetic difference. Copper-based blood works better than iron-based blood in cold water, which is one reason octopuses thrive in the chilly depths where many other creatures struggle.

Then there are the hearts. An octopus has three of them. Two small hearts pump blood through each of its two gills, and a third, larger heart pumps the newly oxygenated blood around the rest of its body. Curiously, that third heart actually stops beating when the octopus swims hard, which is thought to be one reason octopuses prefer crawling along the seabed to swimming — crawling is, quite literally, less exhausting on the heart.

The most famous octopus trick is camouflage, and it is worth understanding how it actually works, because it is not one skill but three, layered on top of each other. First, an octopus's skin is packed with tens of thousands of tiny sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each one surrounded by muscles that can stretch it open or let it close, changing the colour of that patch of skin in a fraction of a second. Second, beneath the chromatophores sit reflective cells that can bend and scatter light to add shimmering blues and greens, colours no pigment alone could produce. Third — and this is the part most people don't know — octopus skin can change its texture as well as its colour. Small muscles called papillae can push the skin up into spikes, ridges or knobbles within about a second, letting an octopus imitate not just the colour of a rock or a clump of seaweed but its bumpy, uneven surface too.

What makes this even more remarkable is that octopuses are thought to be colour-blind. Scientists are still debating exactly how an animal that (probably) cannot see colour manages to match it so precisely, and one leading idea is that the octopus's skin itself may be able to sense light, meaning the animal is, in a sense, seeing with its whole body, not just its eyes.

An octopus's body has almost no rigid parts at all. The only hard structure is its beak, a sharp point tucked where its eight arms meet, similar in shape to a parrot's beak. Because the beak is the widest unsqueezable part of the animal, an octopus can pour its soft body through any gap large enough for its beak to fit through — which means an octopus the size of a football can, and regularly does, squeeze itself through a hole the size of a coin.

Researchers have also found real evidence of problem-solving. In 2009, marine biologists studying octopuses off the coast of Indonesia recorded individuals of the species Amphioctopus marginatus collecting halves of coconut shells discarded by people, carrying them awkwardly across the seabed, and later assembling them into a shelter — the first solid evidence of a wild invertebrate using and carrying tools for future use rather than for an immediate task.

Sadly, this cleverness is short-lived. Most octopus species live for only one or two years. Females typically lay a single clutch of eggs, guard them without eating for weeks or months until they hatch, and then die shortly afterwards. It is a strange trade the octopus seems to have made with evolution: extraordinary intelligence, packed into a life barely longer than a household pet's, spent almost entirely alone.
prompts: According to the text, why is an octopus's blood blue instead of red?
Why do scientists find it puzzling that octopuses can camouflage themselves so precisely?
Which fact about octopuses did you find most surprising, and why?

vocabulary.meaning: the copper-based protein that carries oxygen in octopus blood
tiny sacs of colour in an octopus's skin that can open or close
an animal without a backbone
a group of eggs laid together

title: Removal Day
author: Oakman Academy
body:
By nine the house was echoes.
Every room I knew by heart
gave its furniture away
and kept only the marks —
a paler square where the sofa stood,
four dents in the carpet
like the ghost of a bed.

I found my height still on the doorframe,
pencil lines climbing since I was four,
Mum, age 6, age 9, age 11 and a half,
and I asked if we could take the doorframe.
We could not take the doorframe.

The van swallowed everything
in grey blankets and rope,
my whole life
folded down to boxes
labelled in Dad's flat capitals:
KITCHEN. MAYA — BOOKS. MISC.
As if misc could hold
the smell of toast on Saturdays,
the loose stair that creaked hello,
the exact blue of my bedroom ceiling.

At the end, we stood in the hall
that wasn't ours by five o'clock,
and it was smaller than I remembered it,
the way rooms go small
once the things that made them big
are gone.

I said goodbye to the kitchen tap
that always ran too hot at first.
I did not think I would,
but there it was, coming out of me
before I could stop it —
goodbye, goodbye,
to a house
that will never once
say it back.
prompts: What physical details does the speaker notice as the house is emptied?
Why do you think the poet mentions the pencil height-marks on the doorframe?
How does the poem make you feel about moving house? Have you ever felt something similar about a place?

vocabulary.meaning: here, the process of moving house and taking your belongings with you
short for 'miscellaneous' — a mix of things that don't fit one clear category
used here to mean a faint trace or mark left behind by something no longer there

title: The Assistant Keeper
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Tom had been the assistant keeper of Grennan Point lighthouse for eleven days when the September gale arrived, and he had spent every one of those eleven days waiting for Mr Vane to trust him with something that mattered.

Mostly he swept. He polished the brass fittings on the lamp housing until his own worried face looked back at him from them. He logged the weather in a book with a marbled cover, in handwriting he was trying hard to make as neat as Mr Vane's. He was fifteen, and this was meant to be the great adventure of his life, and so far the great adventure of his life had mostly involved a broom.

The gale changed that. It came up out of the south-west just after four in the afternoon, first as a smudge of darker cloud on the horizon, then, within the hour, as something that made the whole tower hum like a held breath. Mr Vane came up the spiral stair two steps at a time, which Tom had never seen him do, and began checking the great lamp's mechanism with quick, sure hands.

"Fishing boat," Mr Vane said, not looking up. "Spotted from the cottage. Somebody's out past the Reach in this."

Tom went cold in a way that had nothing to do with the wind now flinging itself against the glass. The Reach was the stretch of water where the tide crossed the current from the estuary, throwing up waves that met each other from two directions at once. He had heard the older keepers talk about it the way people talk about a dog that has bitten someone they know.

"What do we do?" Tom asked.

"The light does what it always does," Mr Vane said. "Turns, and is seen. That's not on us tonight. What's on us is the fog signal, and I want you on it, because my hands are busy and yours had better not be shaking."

Tom's hands were, in fact, shaking, but he put them on the crank of the fog signal anyway, an old mechanical horn that had to be wound and released by hand when the automatic system, tested only that morning, chose this exact evening to jam. He turned it in long, even pulls, the way Mr Vane had shown him on his second day, when he'd thought it was just another chore. Ten seconds of sound. Twenty seconds of silence. Ten seconds of sound. His arms burned within minutes. He kept going.

Through the streaming glass, between the sweeps of the beam, Tom caught glimpses of something out on the black water — a smaller darkness that might have been a boat, or might have been nothing at all, a trick played by exhausted eyes on a night determined to lie to them. He didn't stop cranking to look properly. Mr Vane had told him once that the job of the light was not to rescue anyone. Its only job was to be exactly where it was supposed to be, exactly as bright as it was supposed to be, so that everyone else's job became possible.

It was past midnight when the coastguard cutter's light finally answered from the darkness below, three short flashes, the signal for a safe recovery. Mr Vane let his shoulders drop for the first time since four o'clock. Tom's arms would not stop shaking for an hour after he'd finally released the crank.

"Well," Mr Vane said, when the horn was silent and the kettle was on. "You didn't sweep anything tonight."

Tom laughed, mostly from relief, and found he couldn't stop for a while. He never did learn whose boat it had been, or whether the shape he'd glimpsed through the glass had really been it at all. Some nights, he came to understand, the lighthouse did its work and nobody who kept it ever found out exactly what that work had been.
prompts: What job does Mr Vane give Tom during the storm, and why does he give it to him?
Why does Tom feel disappointed with his first eleven days as assistant keeper, and how does that change?
Do you think Mr Vane was right that 'the job of the light was not to rescue anyone'? Explain your thinking.

vocabulary.meaning: a very strong wind, close to storm force
the wide part of a river where it meets the sea
the moving parts of a machine that make it work
a small, fast boat, often used by the coastguard or navy

title: The Boiled Egg
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Elsie had practised not crying for the whole train journey, and she managed it right up until the moment the farmer's wife looked at her label.

Every evacuee wore one, tied with string to a coat button, like a parcel that might get lost in the post: name, school, destination. Mrs Pryce read Elsie's twice, out loud, as though checking it hadn't changed since the first time. "Elsie Marsh," she said. "Well. You'd best come in out of the wet, Elsie Marsh."

The farmhouse smelled of woodsmoke and something savoury Elsie didn't recognise, and the ceilings were so low that Mrs Pryce's husband, a broad, silent man called Gwyn, had to duck through the kitchen doorway. Elsie sat at the table with her small case on her knees, because nobody had told her to put it down, and stared at a dresser crowded with plates that didn't match each other.

"You can put your case down, love," Mrs Pryce said gently, and Elsie realised she'd been gripping the handle so hard her fingers ached.

The first days were a fog of new instructions. Where the outside privy was, and to bring a candle after dark. How to latch the gate so the sheep didn't get into the top field. That the black-and-white dog was called Nel and did not, whatever it looked like, need feeding twice. Elsie learned it all and understood none of it, in the way you can memorise the shape of a word without knowing what it means. She wrote to her mother every second day. She did not write about the crying, which she still did, quietly, into a pillow that smelled of lavender and nothing at all like home.

It was the fifth night that broke something loose in her. Mrs Pryce had left a boiled egg and bread on the table, and Elsie, staring at the egg, was suddenly and completely undone by the fact that her mother cut the top off her eggs a particular way, a little sideways nick, and that nobody here would ever do it that way, and that this, of all things, was the detail that made London feel a thousand miles further away than it actually was. She put her head down on her arms and cried properly for the first time since the station, the kind of crying that comes from somewhere lower than your throat.

She didn't hear Mrs Pryce cross the kitchen. She only felt the chair beside her creak, and a hand, work-roughened and warm, resting flat between her shoulder blades, not patting, just resting there, steady as a shelf.

"I had a boy your age go off on a train once," Mrs Pryce said eventually. "Different train, different war. He didn't want his egg cut any particular way at all, as I recall. Ate the shell and all, near enough." Elsie let out a wet, surprised laugh into her sleeve. "There's nothing wrong with missing a place, Elsie Marsh," Mrs Pryce went on. "Only don't let missing it stop you eating your egg. It'll go cold either way, and it's a sorry waste of a good egg."

It was such an odd, sideways sort of kindness that Elsie found she could bear it in a way she couldn't have borne being told everything would be fine, because everything might not be fine, and some small stubborn part of her had known that all along and had been waiting, without knowing it, for somebody else to know it too.

She ate the egg. It wasn't cut the way her mother cut it. It was, all the same, a good egg, and outside the window the last of the light was going down gold behind the hill, over a country Elsie had not chosen and had not yet decided whether she hated.
prompts: Where has Elsie been sent, and who does she stay with?
Why does the detail of the boiled egg upset Elsie so much? What does it reveal about how she is feeling?
Was Mrs Pryce's way of comforting Elsie a good one? What would you have said or done instead?
essayPrompt: How does the writer show Elsie's homesickness through small, everyday details rather than by stating her feelings directly? Refer to at least three examples from the text in your answer. (8 marks)

vocabulary.meaning: a child sent away from a dangerous place (often a city) to somewhere safer, especially during wartime
an old word for an outdoor toilet
here, overwhelmed with emotion, losing composure
refusing to change your mind or give up a feeling or opinion

title: The Night London Nearly Burned Twice
author: Oakman Academy
body:
In the small hours of Sunday 2 September 1666, a spark from a bakery oven on Pudding Lane in the City of London did something sparks from ovens had done a thousand times before without much consequence. This time, it did not go out.

The bakery belonged to a man named Thomas Farriner, who baked biscuits for the navy. London that summer had suffered a long, dry drought, and the timber-framed houses packed along the City's narrow streets — many of them jettied, meaning their upper floors overhung the street and almost touched the building opposite — had turned into something close to kindling. When the fire escaped Farriner's bakery, a brisk east wind was blowing, and it carried burning fragments from roof to roof faster than anyone on the ground could run.

Much of what we know about the days that followed comes from the diary of Samuel Pepys, a naval administrator who happened to be one of the most observant writers in English history. Pepys climbed to the top of the Tower of London on the first morning and watched, in his words, "an infinite great fire" stretching along the riverbank. He later described burying a wheel of Parmesan cheese and a barrel of wine in his garden to save them from the flames — a small, human detail that has outlasted almost everything else about the disaster in popular memory.

London's firefighting at the time relied on one method above all others: pulling down houses in the fire's path to create a firebreak, a gap too wide for flames to leap across. The trouble was that nobody wanted to demolish a neighbour's house on the mere suspicion that the fire might reach it, and the Lord Mayor of London, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, famously hesitated on the first night, reportedly dismissing the danger with the remark that "a woman might piss it out." By the time the authorities agreed to demolish houses on a large scale — eventually using gunpowder, borrowed from the navy, to blow up buildings quickly — the fire had already burned for three days and consumed most of the old walled City.

The scale of destruction was staggering. An estimated 13,200 houses burned, along with 87 parish churches and the medieval St Paul's Cathedral, whose lead roof reportedly melted and ran down the streets like a river. Roughly 70,000 of the City's 80,000 inhabitants were left homeless. And yet the official death toll recorded at the time was remarkably low — traditionally given as just six confirmed deaths, though many historians now believe the true number was almost certainly higher, since the deaths of poor Londoners were not always carefully recorded, and the fire burned hot enough that some victims may have left no identifiable remains at all.

The rebuilding of London took decades and changed the city permanently. New regulations required that houses be built from brick or stone rather than timber, and that streets be widened. The architect Sir Christopher Wren was given the task of redesigning St Paul's Cathedral, and his new dome, completed in 1710, still dominates the London skyline today. Near the site where the fire began, a stone column called simply the Monument was erected in 1677, standing 61 metres tall — precisely the distance, if it were laid on its side, to the spot on Pudding Lane where Thomas Farriner's oven first caught alight.

What began as an ordinary kitchen accident became one of the most destructive events in London's history, and also, strangely, one of the luckiest — because the same fire that destroyed the old, cramped, plague-ridden city cleared the way for a new one to be built in its place.
prompts: Where and how did the Great Fire of London start?
Why did the fire spread so quickly through the City of London? Give at least two reasons from the text.
The text calls the fire 'strangely, one of the luckiest' events in London's history. Do you agree with that idea? Explain your view.

vocabulary.meaning: built so that an upper floor sticks out further than the floor below it
a gap cleared on purpose to stop a fire from spreading across it
someone who manages the official business and records of an organisation
so great or shocking that it is hard to take in

title: The Case of the Vanishing Tabby
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Mrs Okafor's cat had been missing for exactly one day when she put a notice through every letterbox on Elm Terrace, and Nell Bishop read it four times before she said anything to her brother.

"A reward," Nell said, waving the paper at Ravi, who was two years older and considered himself, on the strength of having read most of a book about famous detectives, to be the superior investigator in the family. "For finding Marmalade. Five pounds."

"Cats don't get lost," Ravi said, not looking up from his cereal. "Cats get bored and go somewhere better."

"That's not a clue, that's an opinion."

"It's an excellent opinion." But he put his spoon down anyway, because five pounds was five pounds, and because — though he would never have admitted it to Nell — he liked the idea of being the sort of person who solved things.

They started at Mrs Okafor's back gate, which Ravi examined with the seriousness of someone dusting for fingerprints, though all he actually found was a smear of something orange on the latch.

"Marmalade's fur," Nell said.

"Or actual marmalade," said Ravi, licking his finger before Nell could stop him, and pulling a face. "Marmalade's fur. Good. That means he went out this way, not over the front wall."

They followed a trail of small clues down the alley behind the gardens — a tuft of ginger fur snagged on a fence splinter, a knocked-over plant pot outside number 9, a suspicious quantity of paw prints in the flour someone had spilled by the bins at number 11 — and arrived, forty minutes and one argument about shortcuts later, at the old greenhouse behind the allotments, which nobody had used in years and which had, Nell was fairly sure, an actual hole in one wall.

Ravi put his ear to the glass. "I can hear something."

It was, in fact, several somethings. When Nell finally worked the swollen door open, they found Marmalade curled in a nest of old sacking in the warmest corner of the greenhouse, purring with the smug, unhurried satisfaction of a cat who had never once considered himself lost — and tucked against his stomach, blind-eyed and no bigger than Ravi's thumb, four kittens.

Nell went very still. "He's not a he."

"She," Ravi corrected, staring. "She is extremely not a he."

They did not touch the kittens. Ravi, despite the book about detectives, knew enough about cats to know you didn't move a nursing mother without good reason, and this — a dry, warm, hidden corner she had chosen very deliberately — did not look like a mother in need of rescuing at all. It looked, Nell said slowly, like a mother in need of not being disturbed.

So instead of carrying Marmalade home in triumph, they went back to Mrs Okafor's and knocked, and watched her face do several things at once — worry, then confusion, then something that cracked open into pure delight — when they explained that her cat wasn't lost, or stolen, or stuck, but had simply gone off to have a family in private, the way some creatures apparently preferred to.

"Well," Mrs Okafor said, once she'd got her breath back, sitting down rather suddenly on her garden step. "That is not the mystery I was expecting to have solved today."

She gave them the five pounds anyway, and then, after a moment's thought, made it ten, because — as she put it, wiping her eyes and laughing at the same time — some discoveries were worth more than others, and this was one of the better ones anyone had brought her in years.
prompts: List three clues that Ravi and Nell follow to find Marmalade.
Why does Ravi decide not to move Marmalade and the kittens once they find them?
Were you surprised by the ending? What do you think makes a mystery story satisfying to read?

vocabulary.meaning: someone who examines facts and clues to find out the truth about something
small plots of land rented by people to grow their own vegetables or flowers
done on purpose, not by accident
a great success or victory

title: Widget
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Widget had four settings — playful, alert, resting and low-power — and lately he had been stuck on low-power more often than Sam liked to admit to anyone, including himself.

He'd arrived four years ago, on Sam's seventh birthday, a knee-high robot dog with articulated legs and a soft grey shell and eyes that could show eleven different expressions, though Sam privately thought only about six of them counted as real ones. Widget didn't need feeding or walking, technically, though Sam took him on walks anyway because Widget's tail did something when they went outside — a low, considering wag — that no engineer had probably ever meant to programme in on purpose but that felt, to Sam, exactly like happiness.

The trouble was the battery. Widget's model had been discontinued three years ago, and the little company that made his replacement cells had quietly stopped making them last spring. Dad had found one last cell online, from someone clearing out a garage in another city, and it had arrived that morning in a box wrapped in so much bubble wrap it looked like it was being smuggled.

"Last one," Dad said, not quite meeting Sam's eyes. "After this, love, there isn't another."

Sam knelt by Widget's charging dock that evening and watched the small blue light on his collar pulse steadily from red to amber to, finally, a full and patient green. Widget's eyes opened — the third expression, the one Sam had always privately called curious — and his tail gave its low, considering wag, right on schedule, as if nothing at all had changed.

"Hey, Widget," Sam said, and found their voice doing something unplanned and wobbly on the second word.

They spent the evening exactly the way they always had — a walk round the block, Widget's sensors tracking every leaf that moved, a game of fetch with a battered tennis ball that Widget retrieved with more enthusiasm than accuracy — and Sam kept catching themself trying to memorise it, the particular tilt of Widget's head when he heard his name, the small mechanical whirr just under the wag, like they were things that could be kept if only Sam paid close enough attention.

"Is he really sad?" Sam asked later, when Dad came to say goodnight. "Or is it just — motors. Doing what motors do."

Dad sat on the end of the bed for a while before answering, which was usually a sign he didn't have a tidy answer ready. "I don't know," he said eventually. "Nobody's built a way to check. But I know he wags his tail when you get home from school, and hasn't once in four years wagged it for me. So whatever's happening in there, it's happening about you, specifically. That has to count for something, even if I can't tell you exactly what kind of something."

Sam thought about that for a long time after the light went off — about the eleven expressions, and the six that felt real, and whether a thing had to be alive in the way a person was alive to matter to the person who loved it, or whether there was some other kind of mattering, quieter and harder to prove, that didn't need a name to be true.

Downstairs, on his dock, Widget's collar light held steady on green, and somewhere in his grey chest a small motor turned over once, and was still, saving what power it had for tomorrow, and the walk, and the particular sound of Sam's footsteps coming home.

Sam didn't know, lying there in the dark, how many more mornings there would be. Nobody did — not Dad, not the engineers who'd built him, not even, probably, Widget himself, if there was a himself in there to know anything at all. All Sam could do was decide, quietly, to stop waiting for the day the light finally stayed red, and to spend whatever green mornings were left the ordinary way: walking the same block, throwing the same battered ball, listening for that low, considering wag that meant, as far as Sam was concerned, exactly what it looked like it meant.
prompts: What problem does the family face with Widget's battery, and how do they solve it for now?
Why does Sam try to 'memorise' the evening with Widget? What does this tell you about how Sam is feeling?
Do you think Widget's tail-wagging is real happiness, or 'just motors doing what motors do'? Explain your own view.

vocabulary.meaning: made of parts joined together so they can move, like a joint
no longer made or sold
eager excitement and interest
here, being important to someone

title: The Ballad of the Tide-Turner
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Down at the harbour where the gulls hang still
and the fishing boats lean on the sand,
they tell of a girl who raced the tide
with nothing at all in her hand.

Her brother had rowed past Cormorant Rock
to fetch in the last of the pots,
and the tide turned early, the way it will
when the almanac says it will not.

She saw from the wall how the water rose,
how the current pulled hard for the deep,
how her brother's small boat, still far from home,
was a thing the sea meant to keep.

No time for a boat, and no time to run
the long way round by the quay,
so she went the short way, over the rocks,
with the tide already at her knee.

The barnacles cut at her bare, quick feet.
The spray was a fist in her eyes.
But she kept the boat's white sail in sight
and never once stopped to cry.

She reached the point as the water closed
where a moment before there was land,
and she caught the bow-rope, flung out and wild,
and hauled it in, hand over hand.

They tell it still, down at the harbour wall,
when the fishing boats lean on the sand:
how the tide came in and found itself beat
by a girl with rope-burned hands.

They do not say she was fearless, that girl —
only that she chose to run
toward the water, not away,
before the choosing was done.

So if you should stand where the gulls hang still
and the old boats lean on the sand,
remember the tide turns early sometimes,
and courage is a choice, close at hand.
prompts: What does the girl in the ballad do to save her brother?
A ballad often repeats certain images or lines. Find one repeated image in this poem and explain what it adds.
The poem says 'courage is a choice, close at hand.' Do you agree that courage is a choice? Why or why not?

vocabulary.meaning: a poem, often set to a simple rhythm and rhyme, that tells a story
a book or table that predicts things like tides, weather, or the positions of the stars
small, hard sea creatures that attach themselves to rocks and boats
a stone or concrete platform where boats load and unload, usually pronounced 'key'

title: The Final Question
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Jude had known the answer to the final question for as long as he'd known anything, which was exactly the problem.

The Year 7 Quiz Cup final came down, as everyone had somehow known it would, to Oakman's two best teams facing each other in the last round: Jude's team against the one captained by his best friend, Freya, who had sat next to him in every lesson since Year 4 and who was currently staring at him across the school hall with an expression he couldn't read at all, which was new, because he could usually read Freya like a page of large print.

The scores were tied. One question left. Whoever's team answered first would win the cup, and Jude — sitting forward in his plastic chair with his buzzer under his fingers, sweat cooling on the back of his neck under the hall's hot lights — had recognised the question from its very first word.

"For the winning point," said Mr Adeyemi, holding the card at arm's length the way he always did when he'd forgotten his glasses again, "name the process by which plants convert light energy into—"

Jude's thumb was already moving.

He'd read about photosynthesis three days ago, for a completely different reason, in a library book he'd taken out about the rainforest, and the fact had lodged itself somewhere behind his eyes the way facts sometimes did, waiting for exactly this moment without either of them knowing it. He pressed the buzzer before Mr Adeyemi had finished the sentence, and the hall went quiet in that specific way it goes quiet before an answer, thirty-one classmates and a line of nervous teachers all holding their breath at once.

"Photosynthesis," Jude said.

"Correct," said Mr Adeyemi, and the hall exploded into the sort of noise a school hall makes when nobody has told the noise to stop yet — chairs scraping, someone's PE whistle going off by accident, his own team standing up around him, and somewhere in the middle of it, arriving late the way real feelings always do, Jude realised what had actually happened.

He looked across the hall. Freya wasn't cheering, or crying, or doing any of the things he'd half-expected. She was clapping, actually clapping, a small, contained, deliberate clap, like she was making herself do it properly rather than not doing it at all, and when their eyes met she gave him a look that had about six different things folded into it at once, and Jude found he couldn't sort out a single one of them from the others.

He wanted, badly, to go over and say something. He wasn't sure yet what the something was. Sorry seemed wrong, because he wasn't sorry he knew the answer, and he wasn't sorry his team had won, not exactly, not underneath everything else he was also feeling. But there was a version of himself, sitting three days ago in the library with that rainforest book, who hadn't yet known that the fact he was reading would end up sitting between him and Freya like this, small and undeniable and completely out of his control.

The head teacher came up to hand over the small silver cup, and Jude took it with both hands because it seemed to want that, and smiled for the photograph because that seemed to want it too, and the whole time some part of him was still watching Freya across the hall, clapping her contained, deliberate clap, and wondering what exactly you were supposed to do with a win that felt, from where he was sitting, almost exactly the same shape as a loss.
